setup: Mali was the second of three great West African gold empires, and to understand it you first have to understand the land and the people it grew out of. The land is the Sahel, a band of semi-arid grassland between the Sahara and the southern savanna, cut by the Niger River — which does something no other major river does, bending north into the desert before curving back south and depositing the Inner Niger Delta, a vast flooded breadbasket in the middle of dry country. That geography set the economy: gold from the south, salt from the north, camel caravans linking the two, and whoever sat in the middle taxing the trade got rich. The first to do it was the Ghana Empire (Wagadu) under the Soninke. By around 1200 Ghana had faded and a power vacuum opened. Into it stepped the Sosso king Sumanguru Kante — remembered in oral tradition as a sorcerer-king — who conquered the still-fragmented Mandinka clans. That domination is what one young Keita prince would rise against.

bridge: Chapter 1 left the upper Niger under foreign domination. The old Ghana Empire had faded, and into the vacuum stepped the Sosso kingdom under Sumanguru Kante, the sorcerer-king of later legend, who absorbed most of Ghana's old territory and pressed south into the homeland of the Mandinka — a network of small clan kingdoms, not yet a unified state, each paying tribute to whoever was strongest. Tradition holds Sumanguru had executed most of the senior Keita princes, leaving one sickly young heir in exile. That heir is where this chapter starts.
setup: In or around 1235, a young Mandinka prince named Sundiata Keita led an alliance of clans against Sumanguru and defeated him at the Battle of Kirina, ending Sosso domination of the upper Niger. He was proclaimed Mansa — emperor — and the Mali Empire began. Sundiata is a figure who hovers between history and myth: the basic political facts (a successful revolt, a multi-clan state under a Keita king) are real, while the famous scenes (the boy who couldn't walk until seven, the magical arrow tipped with a white rooster's spur) belong to the Sundiata epic, oral tradition preserved by the jeli for centuries before being written down. The year after Kirina, Sundiata convened an assembly that produced the Kurukan Fuga, also called the Manden Charter — an oral constitution defining clans, rights, and obligations, promulgated roughly twenty years after Magna Carta and by a completely separate tradition. He founded a capital at Niani and built a three-ring structure that could hold a diverse empire together.

bridge: Chapter 2 founded the empire: Sundiata won at Kirina around 1235, was made Mansa, issued the oral Manden Charter at Kurukan Fuga, and built a capital at Niani and a flexible three-ring administration that let many peoples stay autonomous under Mali rule. He died around 1255 and the throne passed to his son without a major civil war. But a founding is not an institution. Sundiata had set the frame; what held the empire together over the next half-century was the machinery built underneath it.
setup: This chapter is about that machinery — the structural foundations laid between Sundiata's death and the accession of Mansa Musa in 1312. The empire ran on grain from the Inner Niger Delta, where farmers planted African rice along the receding flood. Its power rested on cavalry, which could only exist because Mali sat north of the tsetse-fly belt that kills horses to the south, and a trained warhorse cost the equivalent of several enslaved people, making cavalry an aristocratic monopoly. Its memory rested on the jeli, the hereditary griots whose institutional protection across regime changes preserved the Sundiata epic for eight centuries. And it was held by a string of early successors — Mansa Uli, who made the first recorded Malian hajj; the freed slave-soldier Sakura who seized and legitimately held the throne — keeping the line intact until it reached the most famous ruler of all.

bridge: By the time Chapter 3 closed, Mali was structurally complete: a breadbasket in the Inner Niger Delta, a heavy-cavalry military, a jeli institution preserving imperial memory, a Muslim merchant elite running the trans-Saharan trade, and three generations of functional mansas keeping the Keita line intact. It was the dominant power in West Africa and a major medieval trading state — but outside its immediate trade contacts, almost nobody had heard of it. The European Mediterranean did not even know Mali existed as a distinct place, only that gold kept arriving from somewhere south. One man was about to change that.
setup: Around 1312, Mansa Musa came to the throne, and in the spring of 1324 he set out on the hajj with a caravan the Arabic sources describe as around 60,000 people, twelve thousand slaves carrying gold, and a hundred camels each loaded with gold dust (figures the narrative treats with caution, but the caravan was undeniably enormous). The pilgrimage was the most spectacular hajj in the history of Islam and the most consequential political act of any pre-modern sub-Saharan ruler. In Cairo, Musa gave away so much gold over three months that the gold-to-silver exchange rate collapsed and stayed depressed for over a decade — and he had to borrow money for the trip home. Within a generation the Islamic world knew Mali, and in 1375 the Catalan Atlas drew Musa enthroned with a gold nugget, the first sub-Saharan African ruler to appear on a European map.

bridge: Chapter 4 followed Mansa Musa's 1324 hajj and its aftermath: the Cairo gold crash, Mali's sudden international fame, and the scholars and architects Musa brought home to build an Islamic establishment at Timbuktu, Djenné, and Niani. That recruitment drive was a deliberate state policy, meant to mature over generations into something larger than any one mosque or court. This chapter is where it matured — and where the real Timbuktu finally gets separated from the legend.
setup: For most of the world 'Timbuktu' means the impossibly remote, the end of the line — a European myth from the eighteenth century. The real city was a working trans-Saharan trade hub on the desert's edge with three notable mosques, a thriving manuscript economy, and a scholarly community whose intellectual life outshone the modest town around it. This chapter asks what Timbuktu actually was in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries: the three great mosques (Djinguereber, Sankoré, Sidi Yahya), the master-student teaching system that the term 'Sankoré University' overstates, and the manuscript tradition that survives today as the largest body of pre-colonial sub-Saharan African writing in existence. Its single most valuable outside witness is Ibn Battuta, who spent eight months in Mali in 1352–53 and left a detailed, often critical eyewitness account. By the chapter's end, though, the political tide is turning: in 1468 Sonni Ali of Songhai captures Timbuktu, and the Niger Bend slips from Mali's grasp.

bridge: Chapter 5 ended with the structural turning point: in 1468 Sonni Ali of Songhai captured Timbuktu, and the loss of the Niger Bend began cutting Mali off from the Saharan trade routes that were its economic foundation. The empire's most famous city — and its claim to Islamic civilizational status, built up under Mansa Musa — was now in someone else's hands. That someone was the Songhai Empire, based at Gao, and this chapter is the story of how it ate Mali alive.
setup: Mali did not collapse; it contracted, over most of the fifteenth century, squeezed by a single rival. The Songhai people — speakers of a language distinct from Mandinka — had been on the Niger Bend around Gao for centuries, long a loose Mali tributary, and they consolidated independence as Mali's center weakened. Under Sonni Ali (ruled 1464–1492), Songhai turned from local kingdom into regional empire through near-continuous campaigning, taking Timbuktu in 1468 and Djenné after a long siege ending in 1473 — remembered as a great empire-builder in Sahelian memory and a violent tyrant in the Timbuktu chronicles, both partly true. His successor Askia Muhammad seized the throne in 1493 and built his legitimacy on Islamic patronage, making his own deliberate-echo hajj and obtaining the title Caliph of Sudan. Mali, meanwhile, was confined to its western Mandinka core — but the Keita lineage, the Kurukan Fuga, the jeli, and the Mande language network all survived the eclipse.

bridge: Chapter 6 left Mali contracted to its western Mandinka core, eclipsed by the Songhai Empire, which under Sonni Ali and Askia Muhammad had taken the Niger Bend, Timbuktu, and Djenné and become the dominant power of the western Sahel. Mali survived in reduced form, its lineage and culture intact; Songhai looked unassailable, the great cavalry empire of the region. Then a force came out of the desert that neither empire was prepared for — and it was aimed at Songhai, not Mali.
setup: This chapter is the hinge that finishes the great Sahelian empires. Ahmad al-Mansur, sultan of Morocco, wanted direct control of West Africa's gold and used the ransom windfall from the 1578 Battle of the Three Kings to build an army equipped with matchlock muskets. In 1590 he sent a small expeditionary force of about 4,000 across the Sahara — a crossing previous rulers had dismissed as impossible, and one that killed roughly half the men en route. Led by the Spanish-born eunuch Judar Pasha, the survivors met a Songhai army perhaps ten times their size at Tondibi on March 1591. The muskets and cannon broke the cavalry charges in a single afternoon. It was the first time gunpowder decisively settled a major battle in sub-Saharan Africa. Mali was never attacked directly — but the collapse of Songhai shattered the trans-Saharan trade Mali depended on, and the empire was caught in the wreckage.

bridge: Chapter 7 ended the political empire. The 1591 Moroccan strike at Tondibi destroyed Songhai and shattered the trans-Saharan trade Mali lived on; by the 1620s Mali was a small Mande kingdom, and around 1670 the imperial line that ran from Sundiata in 1235 quietly dissolved into a network of successor states. But empires end in different ways, and what an ending means depends on what you count. The political institution was gone; the culture, the lineages, and the rituals were not. This final chapter is about what survived.
setup: The question here is what an empire's afterlife actually looks like — and Mali's is unusually rich. The Keita royal family relocated to Kangaba, the ancestral homeland, where every seven years the Kamabolon ceremony reroofs a small shrine and selected jeli recite the full Sundiata epic, the canonical text kept alive across nearly thirty generations. In the west, the Kaabu Federation outlasted the imperial center by almost two and a half centuries, falling only at the Battle of Kansala in 1867. The imperial capital Niani has dissolved so completely back into the soil that archaeologists cannot securely find it. And the Timbuktu manuscripts — the largest pre-colonial body of sub-Saharan African writing — survived everything until 2012, when librarian Abdel Kader Haidara's clandestine network smuggled an estimated 350,000 of them to safety. The Manden Charter sits on a UNESCO list; the modern Republic of Mali took the empire's name. The cultural project, it turns out, has lasted nearly twice as long as the political one.
